## Chapter 1

# CHAPTER II

BOSTON (1848–1854)

Peter Chardon Brooks, the other grandfather, died January 1, 1849, bequeathing what was supposed to be the largest estate in Boston, about two million dollars, to his seven surviving children. His daughter Abigail had married Charles Francis Adams in 1829; their fourth child, named Henry Brooks after a favorite brother just lost, was thus, by accident of being of less account, in a way given to his mother.

The Adams connection in Boston was singularly small; the Brooks family, almost wholly of clerical New England stock, was large and brilliant. Innumerable cousins slept through their uncle's sermons at the First Church every Sunday, dimly conscious of feuds two hundred years old that had never ceased. By 1850 the quarrels of John Adams and John Quincy Adams were no longer acutely personal; the game was considered drawn; and Charles Francis Adams might have taken his inherited rights of political leadership in succession to Webster. Instead he drew himself aloof and renewed the old war. He could not help it. With the record of J. Q. Adams fresh in popular memory, his son could not make terms with the slave-power, which overshadowed all the great Boston interests. They were anti-slavery by birth, as their name was Adams and their home was Quincy. Had State Street been Paradise, they must hunger for it in vain.

A few months after the death of John Quincy Adams, a convention of anti-slavery delegates met at Buffalo and named for Vice-President: Charles Francis Adams. The year 1848 was like enough to 1776 to make a fair parallel. The stamp of 1848 was almost as indelible; men whose lives were to fall between 1865 and 1900 had first of all to get rid of it. Nature had given to the boy Henry a character that, in any previous century, would have led him into the Church; he scarcely needed a violent reaction like anti-slavery politics to sweep him back into Puritanism with a violence as great as that of a religious war.

His father's character was the larger part of his education. To his son Henry, the quality that distinguished Charles Francis Adams from all the other figures in the family group was that he possessed the only perfectly balanced mind that ever existed in the name. For a hundred years every newspaper scribbler had derided the older Adamses for want of judgment; they abused Charles Francis for his judgment. He was singular for mental poise — absence of self-assertion — the faculty of standing apart without seeming aware that he was alone — a balance of mind and temper that neither challenged nor avoided notice, nor admitted question of superiority or jealousy, even under great pressure. His mind was not bold like his grandfather's or restless like his father's; but it worked with singular perfection, admirable self-restraint, and instinctive mastery of form.

Almost alone among his Boston contemporaries, he was not English in feeling. Royalty itself seemed nothing more than a slightly inconvenient presence. Never did his son see him flatter or vilify, or show a sign of envy or vanity. The critics called him cold. Average human nature is very coarse, and its ideals must necessarily be average. The world never loved perfect poise. Napoleons and Andrew Jacksons amuse it; it is not amused by perfect balance. Between party discipline and secession, he set up a party of his own.

Its social centre was the house in Mount Vernon Street; the group numbered three: Dr. Palfrey, Richard H. Dana, and Charles Sumner. Palfrey had wit; Dana, vigorous and aristocratic to the tenth generation, forced himself to take life as it came, suffocating his longings by mere force of will. Sumner adored English standards and aimed at the career of Edmund Burke. Having sacrificed his social position in America to principle, he clung the more closely to foreign attachments, and was rarely without a pocket-full of letters from duchesses. He was socially ostracized, and though the most socially ambitious of all, could enter hardly half-a-dozen houses in Boston. The boy Henry worshipped him. To the twelve-year-old, his father, Palfrey, Dana, were men more or less like what he himself might become; but Sumner was a different order — heroic.

Winter after winter, the boy worked over his Latin Grammar at a writing-table in the alcove of his father's library, and listened to these gentlemen discussing anti-slavery politics. They were statesmen, not politicians; they guided public opinion, but were little guided by it. The boy took for granted that this sort of world was the one he was to fit. The system had proved so successful that Germany wanted to try it, and Italy yearned for it. England's middle-class government was the ideal of human progress.

No one, except Karl Marx, foresaw radical change. The world was producing sixty or seventy million tons of coal, and might be using nearly a million steam-horsepower, just beginning to make itself felt. All experience conspired to deceive a twelve-year-old boy who took for granted that his ideas, alone respectable, would be alone respected. Politics offered no difficulties; the moral law was a sure guide. Social perfection was sure, because human nature worked for Good, and three instruments were all she asked — Suffrage, Common Schools, and Press:

"Were half the power that fills the world with terror,
Were half the wealth bestowed on camps and courts,
Given to redeem the human mind from error,
There were no need of arsenals nor forts."

Nothing quieted doubt so completely as the mental calm of the Unitarian clergy. They proclaimed as their merit that they insisted on no doctrine, but taught the means of leading a virtuous, useful, unselfish life. Difficulties might be ignored; doubts were waste of thought; nothing exacted solution. Boston had solved the universe.

Of all the conditions of his youth that afterwards puzzled him, this disappearance of religion puzzled him most. The boy went to church twice every Sunday; he read his Bible; he prayed; he went through all the forms; but neither to him nor to his brothers and sisters was religion real. The religious instinct had vanished, and could not be revived, though one made in later life many efforts to recover it. That the most powerful emotion of man, next to the sexual, should disappear, might be a personal defect; but that the most intelligent society, led by the most intelligent clergy, should have solved all the problems of the universe so thoroughly as to have quite ceased making itself anxious about past or future, seemed to him the most curious social phenomenon he had to account for in a long life.

The children reached manhood without knowing religion, and with the certainty that dogma, metaphysics, and abstract philosophy were not worth knowing. So one-sided an education could have been possible in no other country or time, but it became almost of necessity the more literary and political.

## Chapter 2

By way of educating and amusing the children, Mr. Adams read aloud, especially when satirical, like the speeches of Horace Mann and the "Epistles" of Hosea Biglow. The children took possession of Dickens and Thackeray for themselves; both were too modern for tastes founded on Pope and Dr. Johnson. The boy Henry became a desultory reader of every book he found readable, but these were commonly eighteenth-century historians, his father's library being full of them. He read shelves of eighteenth-century poetry, but when his father offered his own set of Wordsworth as a gift on condition of reading it through, he declined. Pope and Gray called for no mental effort; the boy was thirty before his education reached Wordsworth.

This is the story of an education, and the persons who figure in it have value only as educators or educated. The boy had a large and overpowering set of brothers and sisters, modes or replicas of the same type, getting the same education, struggling with the same problems, and solving the question, or leaving it unsolved, much in the same way. They amounted to one individual with half-a-dozen sides; their temperaments reacted on each other and made each child more like the other.

By some happy chance they grew up to be decent citizens, but Henry Adams, as a brand escaped from the burning, always looked back with astonishment at their luck. Home influences alone never saved the New England boy from ruin. If school helped, it was only by reaction. The dislike of school was so strong as to be a positive gain. He hated it because he was there with a crowd of other boys and compelled to learn by memory a quantity of things that did not amuse him. He always reckoned his school-days, from ten to sixteen years old, as time thrown away. For success in the life imposed on him he needed, as afterwards appeared, the facile use of only four tools: Mathematics, French, German, and Spanish. He never controlled any one of them.

Boston offered few healthy resources for boys or men. Books remained, as in the eighteenth century, the source of life; but the happiest hours of the boy's education were passed in summer lying on a musty heap of Congressional Documents in the old farmhouse at Quincy, reading "Quentin Durward," "Ivanhoe," and "The Talisman," and raiding the garden at intervals for peaches and pears. On the whole he learned most then.

## Chapter 3

# CHAPTER III

WASHINGTON (1850–1854)

Mount Vernon Street had the merit of leaving the boy-mind supple, free to turn with the world. Boston offered no standards that could help outside; from women, the boy got the domestic virtues and nothing else. The garden of Eden was hardly more primitive.

To balance this virtue, the Puritan city had always hidden a darker side. Blackguard Boston was only too educational, and to most boys much the more interesting; it had the charm of force and freedom and superiority to culture or decency. One might fear it, but no one honestly despised it. The commonest boy-game of winter was a snowball battle of the Latin School against all comers on Boston Common; in the dark a stick or stone was as effective as a knife. Ten or twelve years afterwards, when these same boys were fighting and falling on the battle-fields of Virginia and Maryland, Henry wondered whether their education on Boston Common had taught them how to die.

If violence were a part of complete education, Boston was not incomplete. Mobs were always possible. Worst of all, the execution of the Fugitive Slave Law in Boston — the sight of Court Square packed with bayonets, and his own friends obliged to line the streets under arms as State militia, in order to return a negro to slavery — wrought frenzy in the brain of a fifteen-year-old, eighteenth-century boy from Quincy.

In May, 1850, his father took him to Washington to visit his bedridden grandmother, the Madam. The journey was meant as education. What struck him most, to remain fresh in his mind all his lifetime, was the sudden change that came over the world on entering a slave State. The railway rambled through unfenced fields among a haphazard variety of pigs, cows, and negro babies, who might all have used the cabins for pens and styes, but who never showed a sign of care.

Slavery struck him in the face; it was a nightmare; a horror; a crime; the sum of all wickedness! And yet the picture had another side. The thickness of foliage, the heavy smells, the brooding indolence of a warm climate, the indolent Southern drawl, the freedom, openness, swagger, of nature and man, soothed his Johnson blood. With him the feeling caught on to an inheritance. He was not sure that he enjoyed the Boston world most.

His father took him to the Capitol and on the floor of the Senate. Clay and Webster and Calhoun were there still. Senators were a species; they all wore an air; they were Roman. Southern pomposity, when not arrogant, was genial and sympathetic, almost quaint and childlike — quite a different thing from the Websterian pomposity of the North. Decidedly the Senate, pro-slavery though it were, seemed a friendly world.

He was taken to see President Taylor. Outside, "Old Whitey," the President's charger, was grazing; inside, the President was receiving callers as simply as if he were in the paddock too. The boy felt no sensation whatever before Presidents. A President was a matter of course in every respectable family; he had two in his own. Any one could be President, and some very shady characters were likely to be.

Mr. Adams took the boy to Mount Vernon in a carriage and pair, over a road that gave him a complete Virginia education for use ten years afterwards. To the New England mind, roads, schools, clothes, and a clean face were connected as part of the law of order. Bad roads meant bad morals. The moral of this Virginia road was clear: slavery was wicked, and slavery was the cause of this road's badness which amounted to social crime — and yet, at the end of the road, stood Mount Vernon and George Washington.

Luckily boys accept contradictions as readily as their elders do. He had only to repeat what he was told — that George Washington stood alone. He was a primary, or, if Virginians liked it better, an ultimate relation, like the Pole Star; and amid the endless restless motion of every other visible point in space, he alone remained steady, in the mind of Henry Adams, to the end. Mount Vernon was only Quincy in a Southern setting.

The boy went back to Boston more political than ever, and his politics were no longer so modern as the eighteenth century, but took a strong tone of the seventeenth. Slavery drove the whole Puritan community back on its Puritanism. The Slave power took the place of Stuart kings and Roman popes.

The first vague sense of feeling an unknown living obstacle in the dark came in 1851. The Free Soil conclave in Mount Vernon Street belonged to the statesman class, and had nothing to do with machinery. The small Free Soil machine negotiated a bargain with the Massachusetts Democrats giving the State to the Democrats and a seat in the Senate to the Free Soilers. With this bargain Mr. Adams and his statesman friends would have nothing to do; the coalition was in their eyes much like jockeys selling a race. But they took the benefit of the sale, for the coalition chose Charles Sumner as its candidate. The boy might ignore the question how to deduce George Washington from the sum of all wickedness, but he had himself helped to deduce Charles Sumner from the sum of political corruption. Tammany Hall stood at the end of the vista.

Day after day, the General Court balloted; the boy haunted the gallery, following the roll-call. At last, April 24, 1851, Henry heard the vote announced which gave Sumner the needed number. He ran home as hard as he could and burst into the dining-room where Mr. Sumner sat at table with the family. He enjoyed the glory of telling Sumner that he was elected; it was probably the proudest moment in the life of either.

Thus, before he was fifteen years old, he had got himself into a state of moral confusion from which he never escaped. As a politician, he was already corrupt, and he never could see how any practical politician could be less corrupt than himself.

He felt himself shut out of Boston as though he were an exile; always he felt himself somewhere else, and watched from the Quincy hills the smoke of the Cunard steamers stretching in a long line to the horizon and disappearing every other Saturday, as though the steamers were offering to take him away, which was precisely what they were doing.

The only idea which would have been quite unreasonable scarcely entered his mind — that of going westward and growing up with the country. Neither to a politician nor to a business-man did the West promise any certain advantage, while it offered uncertainties in plenty.

He finished with school, not very brilliantly, but without finding fault with the sum of his knowledge. Only on looking back, fifty years later, did he wonder whether the boy of 1854 stood nearer to the thought of 1904, or to that of the year 1. In essentials — religion, ethics, philosophy; history, literature, art; the concepts of all science, except perhaps mathematics — the American boy of 1854 stood nearer the year 1 than to the year 1900. The education he had received bore little relation to the education he needed. Speaking as an American of 1900, he had as yet no education at all. He knew not even where or how to begin.
